seo_title: What Is Hazard Insurance? Home Coverage Explained (2026)
meta_description: What is hazard insurance? What it covers and excludes, how it differs from homeowners insurance, and why lenders require it.
h1: What Is Hazard Insurance for a Home? Coverage, Costs and Texas Tips
excerpt: What is hazard insurance? It is the dwelling coverage in your homeowners policy that lenders require. Learn what it covers, what it excludes and what Texas homeowners should check.
key_takeaways: Hazard insurance is the dwelling coverage within a homeowners policy, not a separate product.
It covers fire, wind, hail, lightning and similar sudden damage to the structure.
Flood, earthquake, wear and tear and sewer backup are generally excluded.
Lenders require it for the life of the mortgage and may force-place coverage if it lapses.
Texas homeowners should check wind/hail deductibles, roof endorsements and coastal windstorm coverage.
body_html:
Hazard insurance is the part of a homeowners insurance policy that pays to repair or rebuild the physical structure of your home after damage from covered perils such as fire, wind, hail, lightning and vandalism. It is not a separate policy. Mortgage lenders use the term "hazard insurance" for the dwelling coverage they require you to carry.

What is hazard insurance?

Hazard insurance is a lender's name for the dwelling coverage in your homeowners policy, usually listed as Coverage A. It protects the house itself: the roof, walls, foundation, windows, built-in fixtures and attached structures like an attached garage. If a covered event damages those parts of your home, hazard coverage pays to repair or replace them, subject to your deductible and limits.

The name comes from mortgage lending. Lenders and loan servicers have long used "hazard insurance" to describe coverage against physical hazards to the collateral, as opposed to coverages like liability that do not protect the loan. The term stuck in loan paperwork even though insurers sell the coverage as part of a homeowners policy.

The term causes confusion because you will rarely see a product called "hazard insurance" for sale. When your lender, title company or loan officer asks for proof of hazard insurance, they are asking for a homeowners policy with enough dwelling coverage to protect the collateral for your loan.

What is hazard insurance in plain terms?

  • What it is: the structure-protection portion of homeowners insurance
  • Who requires it: virtually every mortgage lender
  • What it protects: your home's physical structure, not your belongings or liability
  • Who it protects: you and your lender, who is usually named as mortgagee on the policy

What does hazard insurance cover?

Hazard coverage applies to sudden, accidental physical damage from covered perils. Depending on the policy form, the dwelling may be covered on a named-peril basis (only listed causes) or an open-peril basis (any cause not specifically excluded). Most standard homeowners policies cover these hazards:

  • Fire and smoke, including damage from firefighting efforts
  • Wind and hail, the most common causes of Texas roof claims
  • Lightning, including structural damage from strikes
  • Explosion
  • Vandalism and malicious mischief, often with limits on vacant homes
  • Falling objects, such as trees and large limbs
  • Vehicle and aircraft impact
  • Weight of ice, snow or sleet
  • Sudden and accidental water discharge from plumbing or appliances, subject to policy conditions

What does hazard insurance not cover?

Knowing the exclusions matters as much as knowing the coverage. Standard hazard coverage generally excludes:

  • Flood and rising water, including storm surge
  • Earth movement, such as earthquakes, sinkholes and settling
  • Sewer or drain backup, unless you add an endorsement
  • Wear and tear, deterioration and poor maintenance
  • Pest damage from termites, rodents and insects
  • Mold from long-term leaks, often excluded or capped
  • Personal belongings, which fall under the personal property section, not hazard coverage

For flood protection, homeowners typically buy a policy through the FEMA National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood carrier. Many Texas homeowners outside mapped flood zones skip it and find out after a storm that their hazard coverage does not apply.

Tip: Ask your agent for the exclusions page, not just the declarations page. The exclusions and endorsements decide what your hazard insurance really pays.

Hazard insurance vs homeowners insurance: what's the difference?

Hazard insurance is one piece of homeowners insurance. A full homeowners policy bundles several coverages, and hazard coverage is the dwelling section your lender cares about most.

Hazard insurance vs mortgage insurance

These are often confused but have nothing in common. Hazard insurance pays to repair your home after damage. Private mortgage insurance protects the lender if you stop making payments. You can be required to carry both, but only hazard coverage helps after a storm.

Hazard insurance vs home warranty

A home warranty is a service contract that covers repair or replacement of systems and appliances that break down from normal use. Hazard insurance covers sudden physical damage from events like hail or fire. One does not replace the other.

How hazard insurance works with your mortgage

Your home secures your loan, so the lender requires proof of hazard coverage before closing and for the life of the loan. The lender is listed as mortgagee, which is why claim checks are often made out to both you and your mortgage company.

  1. Before closing, you choose a carrier and provide proof of coverage, usually a declarations page or binder.
  2. Through escrow, many lenders collect the premium monthly with your mortgage payment and pay the insurer each year.
  3. At renewal, the lender expects continuous coverage. A lapse can trigger lender-placed (force-placed) insurance, which typically costs more and protects mainly the lender's interest.
  4. After a claim, large repair checks may be deposited with the lender and released in stages as repairs progress.

How much hazard insurance do you need?

Lenders usually require dwelling coverage at least equal to the loan balance or the cost to rebuild, whichever their guidelines specify. The smarter target is your home's full replacement cost, meaning what it would cost to rebuild at today's labor and material prices. That number is different from your purchase price or market value, because land is not included and construction costs change.

What affects the cost of hazard insurance?

Because hazard coverage is priced inside your homeowners premium, the same factors drive both. Insurers typically weigh:

  • Location, including hail, wind, wildfire and coastal exposure
  • Rebuild cost, based on square footage, construction type and finishes
  • Roof age and material, with credits in some cases for impact-resistant shingles
  • Claims history on the property and for the policyholder
  • Deductibles, especially the percentage wind/hail deductible
  • Protective features, such as monitored alarms and proximity to a fire station

Raising a deductible lowers the premium, but it also raises what you pay out of pocket after every storm. Choose a deductible you could comfortably cover tomorrow.

Hazard insurance in Texas: what homeowners should know

Texas homeowners face a wider range of hazards than most. Hail and severe thunderstorms hit North and Central Texas every spring, hurricanes threaten the Gulf Coast, and wildfire is a growing risk in the Hill Country and West Texas.

Windstorm coverage on the coast

In designated coastal areas, many private carriers exclude wind and hail. Homeowners there often buy windstorm coverage from the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) alongside their homeowners policy, plus separate flood coverage. If you live near Galveston, Corpus Christi or other coastal communities, confirm that your hazard coverage actually includes wind. Our guide to hurricane damage insurance covers this in more detail.

Wind and hail deductibles

Many Texas policies carry a separate wind/hail deductible written as a percentage of dwelling coverage, such as 1 or 2 percent. On a home insured for $350,000, a 2 percent deductible is $7,000, so check this number before storm season.

Roof endorsements

Some Texas carriers pay older roofs on an actual cash value basis or a payment schedule. That can cut a hail claim payout sharply. Understanding recoverable depreciation helps you see what your roof coverage really pays.

How to file a hazard insurance claim

When a covered event damages your home, a fast and organized claim makes the biggest difference.

  1. Protect the property from further damage with tarps or temporary repairs, and keep the receipts.
  2. Report the loss promptly. Our article on the notice of loss explains what to include.
  3. Document everything with photos, video and a written timeline. Use our claim documentation checklist.
  4. Meet the adjuster and walk every damaged area, including the attic and interior ceilings.
  5. Get an independent estimate from a qualified contractor or estimator.
  6. Compare line by line before you accept the carrier's numbers.

Texas law sets timelines for carriers to acknowledge, investigate and pay claims under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 542). This is general information, not legal advice.

What to do when a hazard insurance claim is underpaid

Most hazard claims are approved, but the amount is where disputes happen. Common problems include hail damage labeled cosmetic, missing roof components, low labor pricing and excessive depreciation.

If the dispute is about how much the damage costs to repair, most Texas homeowners policies include an appraisal clause. Each side hires an independent appraiser, and an umpire settles any remaining differences. Read what is an insurance appraisal to see how the process works.

Next steps: review your hazard coverage before you need it

Pull out your declarations page this week. Confirm your dwelling limit reflects today's rebuilding cost, check your wind/hail deductible, look for roof endorsements and note what is excluded. If you live in a flood-prone or coastal area, confirm whether you need flood or windstorm coverage.

Hazard insurance is the coverage that rebuilds your home. Understanding it now means fewer surprises when a Texas storm arrives.

faqs.q: Is hazard insurance the same as homeowners insurance?
faqs.a: Not exactly. Hazard insurance is the dwelling portion of a homeowners policy that covers the structure of your home. A homeowners policy also includes personal property, liability, loss of use and other structures coverage. When a lender asks for hazard insurance, a standard homeowners policy with adequate dwelling coverage almost always satisfies the requirement.

faqs.q: Is hazard insurance required by law in Texas?
faqs.a: No Texas law requires homeowners to carry hazard insurance on a home they own outright. However, nearly every mortgage lender requires it as a loan condition because the house secures the loan. If you let coverage lapse while you have a mortgage, your lender can buy lender-placed coverage and add the cost to your payment.

No. Standard hazard coverage excludes flood, rising water and storm surge. To protect against flooding you need a separate policy through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood insurer. Lenders require flood insurance for homes in certain high-risk flood zones, but homes outside those zones can still flood.

faqs.q: How much does hazard insurance cost?
faqs.a: Because hazard coverage is part of a homeowners policy, its cost is built into your homeowners premium. The price depends on your home's location, age, roof type and condition, rebuild cost, claims history and chosen deductibles. Texas premiums tend to run higher than in many states because of frequent hail, wind and hurricane exposure.

faqs.q: Does hazard insurance cover roof damage?
faqs.a: Yes, hazard coverage generally pays for roof damage caused by covered perils such as hail, wind, falling trees and fire. It does not cover a roof that is simply old or worn out. Some Texas policies limit roof payments with actual cash value or payment schedule endorsements, so check your policy for roof-specific terms.
